Introduction - April 2011 











##### **High prices, but higher risk** 

The base metal sector performed strongly in March, and in early April holding on to the bulk of the gains seen in the earlier part of the year.  The GFMS Base Metal Index averaged 384 in March compared to 398 in February and 361 in January.   The whole of the base metals sector continues to be supported by the investment sector, which retains its long-side bias. 

Our discussions with the downstream fabricators and producers suggest that the demand strength see

n in 2010 has been carried over to the first quarter of this year.  The consumption growth seen in 2010 can essentially be seen as a reaction to the collapse in demand in late 2008 and in 2009.  For consumption growth to be maintained, there has to be support from the key economies.  Aside from China, we doubt whether this will be the case over the second half. 

aluminium price, which has had little or no support from the fundamentals.  Even looking forward, we still project that the market will be in significant surplus this year. 

The gains in nickel prices are hard to explain given the expected surge in production.  The key factor about nickel supply is that the increase is coming from a variety of sources – Chinese nickel pig iron, the recovery from strikerelated losses at Vale’s Canadian operations, the next generation of HPAL projections and the commissioning of ferronickel projects (mainly in Brazil).  The bottom line is that the nickel industry is unlikely to see a repeat of the late 1990s, when the source of extra nickel was from the untried and untested first generation of HPAL projects in Western Australia.  Hence, we retain our cautious stance towards the nickel market. 

In terms of the higher risks towards the sector, there are a number of issues.  First is the sustainability of the economic recovery with some indicators pointing to a slowdown of growth.  Second, we believe that the tragic events in Japan will have a negative impact on the sector.  We do not expect a repeat of the quick rebound in industrial output that occurred following the Kobe earthquake inn 1995. 

As detailed in the individual sections of this report, prices for all the base metals are well in excess of the marginal costs of production.  Also the relationship between LME inventories and prices for most of the metals is being stretched to the right i.e. it is moving far away from the historical norm. 

Although we accept that this relationship has changed, primarily due to the growing acceptance of industrial commodities as an asset class, we still believe that there has to be some fundamental support to justify the current inflated levels.  Even for the markets, which have the most positive fundamentals – in our view copper and tin – the question is whether the fundamentals justify even higher price levels, or a consolidation of the massive price advances seen over the last 18 months.  Our general view favours the latter with our price projections for copper and tin only suggesting the scope for limited advances from the levels prevailing in early April. 

High oil prices have the ability to derail the economic recovery as do the inflationary pressures associated with higher food prices.  The next move for interest rates globally seems to be higher.  These pressures are taking place against the backdrop of fiscal tightening in a number of countries and the re-emergence of the sovereign debt problems in Europe. 

Given the current elevated base metal prices,

GFMS believes that a constant stream of “bullish” news is required to support these levels. Given the concerns highlighted above, we do not believe that this “news flow” will be maintained and we are cautious about the prospects for further price increases. Given that industrial commodities are increasingly seen as an asset class the issue of “relative price performance ” has become more important. Economic Indicators - April 2011 











In Europe, as the Eurozone economic sentiment indicator illustrates, the overall sentiment slightly eased to 107.3 in March, from the recent peak level of 107.9 recorded in February.  The Eurozone economic recovery has helped lift consumer and business sentiment, largely contributed by the mainstream economies, notably Germany, where firms benefited from trading with emerging markets.  Nonetheless, rising inflationary pressures and risks of trade from Japan have ebbed confidence slightly in the future months. 

Japan’s industrial production saw further rise month-onmonth in February.  The country had achieved a

solid start this year, with production, exports and confidence all rebounding after slumping in the second half of 2010. However, sever infrastructure damage and disrupted production stemming from the earthquake and tsunami are expected to weigh on business and consumer confidence and economic output in the near term. So far, most Japanbased auto manufacturers have temporarily idled production in the aftermath of the natural disaster due to power supply issues and parts shortages. The situation of power outages is expected to last through April according to the Japanese officials. Thus, the loss of production output will drag down economic growth in the first two quarters this year. The Chinese growth was still upbeat, shown as significant increases in both industrial production and fixed asset investment, being 14.9% and 24.9% year-on-year in February for each. The near 15% expansion in industrial output outperformed the growth seen last year, despite tightening measures taking hold. Looking at specific industries in more detail, a building boom has been found in China in early 2011, benefiting a wide range of sectors relevant to constructions. Moreover, consumer electronics production has been growing strongly in particular, well supported by exports, and increasingly by robust domestic demand. The acceleration in Chinese fixed asset investment in early 2011 was somewhat unexpected as the tightening monetary policies, being a combination of higher interest rates, increased bank reserve ratios, and further administrative controls over bank lending, were even more seriously implemented by the state, in a bid of tackling inflation pressures as well as cooling real estate investment. Nonetheless, high business sentiment in sectors other than property will still sustain a solid growth in the medium term. ###### **Market outlook** With full year ILZSG data available, GFMS have undertaken a revision of our supply demand projections. Importantly, GFMS continue to see lead as one of the better placed base metals from a fundamental position and, in line with this, we remain constructive towards prices going forward. Our revised full year average price of $2,620/tonne is up from our previous forecast, largely in line with the higher base. The revision is also in part reflective of a more positive fundamental outlook than previously. Indeed, our projections show the lead market in a small deficit of 27,000 tonnes in 2011, revised from our small surplus detailed in our last forecast. This is largely in line with the adjustments made to 2010 figures, with the 2010 surplus reported by the ILZSG smaller than our initial estimation. Over the short term, whilst we have accounted for some further upside as the market continues to react to the recent spate of bullish developments, we believe that a correction from such levels will materialise at some point over the second quarter. Indeed, although bullish on lead’s mediumterm fundamental outlook, we note that LME stocks remain at relatively high levels following the surge over the start of the year and we continue to expect that the market will remain in surplus over the second quarter of 2011. Consequently, and in line with an expected dip amongst the complex from current overheated levels, GFMS would not be surprised to see prices fall back to around $2,400/tonne at some point over the current quarter. Thereafter,

we expect lead’s fundamentals to tighten as the market outside of China posts a notable deficit in light of the ongoing recovery in the respective auto markets and limited increases to refined production. This is expected to lead to a steady drawdown of LME inventories over the second half. Strong Chinese auto demand will also continue to be a key driver, although the extent of the global deficit will however be restricted by the ongoing expansion in Chinese production capacity, with any sustained period of high prices on the Chinese market likely to be met by a strong supply response. Overall, we see the market in a deficit of around 45,000 tonnes over the second half of the year, which will support average prices of $2,620/tonne in the third quarter and $2,650/tonne in the fourth quarter. This bullish trend will continue into 2012 as prices rise to $2,700/tonne over the first quarter, buoyed by a continued tightening of the metal’s fundamental position. There are a number of risks to our base case. The direct hit that has been observed so far was derived from the temporary closure of some tinplate plants and parts of the electronics manufacturing sector, which represents a vital component in global tin consumption.  Moreover, the disruption out of industries relevant to electronic applications, the auto sector for instance, may further constrain tin demand, exemplified by the announcement of output cuts at industry giants due to parts shortages. 

###### **Mining ban lifted in the DRC, with the United States’ law following up** 

In early March, the Congolese government lifted the mining suspension which had been enforced in the key mining areas since last September.  However, the resumption of mining industries is not expected to progress smoothly as the regulation from the United States has come into place from the beginning of April, stipulating the members (including American electronics giants) of the Electronics Industry Citizenship Coalition (EICC) verify that minerals sourced from the DRC and its neighbour countries are “conflict free”. Although we note that the iTSCi traceability programme has made strides in attempting to trace the origins of tin from the area, the “conflict minerals” debate continues to pose downside risk to African tin production going forward. 

###### **Japan crisis poses downside risk to demand** 

In the mature economies, after a rapid rebound in 2010, GFMS are expecting only minimal growth in consumption this year.  It must be stressed that, although this is in part due to a moderation in growth in the United States and EU-27, it is largely due to the expected fall in Japanese demand in light of the recent natural disaster. 

Having said this, the extent of the fall on global tin demand will in part be limited by the fact that electronics manufacturing orders within Japan can potentially be taken by foreign competitors or subsidiary companies located overseas.  Moreover, PT Timah delivered a positive signal in that it maintained shipment to Japan in March, without cancellation of orders from Japanese buyers.  As we note in the market outlook section, we continue to expect that tin will see a significant deficit this year in spite of any potential reduction in Japanese demand. 

###### **Electronics industry will continue to boost Chinese consumption** 

The WBMS estimates that global consumption rose 15.3% year-on-year in January 2011, largely due to an increase in Chinese consumption.  Looking at the end use industries in China, output of the main electronic products enjoyed healthy growth according to the data released by China’s National Bureau of Statistics.  Nonetheless, as a number of Japanese subsidiary enterprises for parts assembly are set in China, electronic products output may face a drop in the upcoming months due to the shortage of parts shipped from Japan.
